wet.label: Wet season
wet.summary: South Kona's rain comes in the afternoon and builds through spring and summer here — the reverse of most of Hawaiʻi's Nov–Mar wet season. This is the site's main planting and active-growth stretch.
tips: Main planting window for both of this site's flagship crops: kalo goes in April through September, ʻōlena (turmeric) March through June.

Rain-fed and not irrigating? Don't plant kalo after the first rain of the season — wait for the second. A single early shower can be a false start; the second confirms the season has really turned and gives roots enough sustained moisture to establish.

Weed early. Pressure on new plantings is highest in the first two to three months — for kalo, letting weeds go during this stretch can cut yield by half or more. Established canopy does most of the weeding for you after that.
The rain does the watering. An on-schedule wet-season planting needs little to no supplemental irrigation through this stretch — the practical payoff of planting on-season instead of against it.

dry.label: Dry season
dry.summary: Cooler and drier, with some species going semi-dormant — the stretch that sets up the next wet season's growth.
tips: Harvest window for ʻōlena: dig roots January through March, and stop watering at least a month before — wet soil at harvest invites rot.
Kalo tells you when it's ready on its own — watch for the big leaves to start dying back and shrinking as the plant redirects energy into the corm.

Cold, not rain, is the real disease risk for ʻōlena this time of year — cold conditions raise the risk of rhizome rot. Worth keeping that distinction straight when deciding what's actually stressing a planting.

Coffee throughout this belt goes semi-dormant now, then blooms once a real rain breaks the dry spell — usually January through May, heaviest in February and March. A visible sign the wet season is on its way back.

events.label: ʻōlena harvest window
events.note: Dig roots now — stop watering at least a month out, and don't harvest into wet soil.

events.label: Coffee bloom (“Kona snow”)
events.note: Look for white blossoms after the next real rain breaks a dry spell — heaviest in February and March.

source_note: Season timing and tips verified 2026-08-25 against the UH Rainfall Atlas of Hawaiʻi, CTAHR's Hawaiʻi Turmeric Production Guidelines (VC-9), the USDA NRCS Plant Guide for taro (COES), and the Hawaiʻi ʻUlu Cooperative's upland kalo growing guide.
